---
name: slow-hook-real-causes
description: Hook latency ground truth — redaction was the tail (fixed, #2002); the ~3s p50 floor is still unexplained but now instrumented
metadata:
  type: project
---

Measured 2026-08-13, updated 2026-08-21 after the fixes landed. Methodology rules
in [[hook-benchmark-methodology]] — measure in a non-CLI repo with a compiled
binary, never in the CLI repo.

## What was wrong, and what shipped

**The tail: redaction, not go-git object I/O.** Profiling
`createRedactedBlobFromFile` put redaction at **99.7%** of the checkpoint blob
write (git object writing was 174ms of a 66.7s pass on 70MB), and the CPU profile
put **82%** of that in betterleaks' regex ruleset. Worse, `full.jsonl` holds the
full session and was re-redacted from byte zero every checkpoint, so a session
with N checkpoints re-redacted O(N^2) bytes — which is also what inflated those
multi-GB packs.

Shipped in **#2002**: shard the per-line pass across goroutines (byte-balanced
~1MiB shards, gated on an explicit `concurrencySafe` arg describing the redactor),
plus reuse the previous checkpoint's redacted prefix and redact only appended
lines. A 14-checkpoint session growing to 70MB went from ~66s to ~2.0s on the
final Stop. Also shipped: **#1984** (slow root perf spans log at WARN — see
[[slow-hook-instrumentation]]), **#1985** (shared go-git object cache, ~2%), and
**#2006** (an unrelated login TTY race that was blocking CI, see
[[ci-race-in-login-tty]]).

## The ~3s p50 floor is STILL OPEN

Real `turn-end` → shadow-commit spans from Stefan's own INFO logs: **p50 3248ms**
across 1383 samples on 2026-08-21, versus 3360ms across 1363 when first measured.
Essentially unmoved — but #2002 merged 2026-08-20 21:05, so nearly all of that
sample predates it. **Do not read the flat aggregate as "the fix didn't work".**

Recent days do look better (08-19: p50 2337ms, 0 of 27 spans ≥3s; 08-20: p50
2583ms, 1 of 16), against an original distribution that was bimodal with roughly
half the invocations ≥3s. But that predates #2002 too, so it is more likely a
workload shift than a fix. Unattributed either way.

**Next step is cheap now:** the WARN instrumentation has already captured 97 slow
traces, and they name the step. Dominant step by count: `push_checkpoint_refs` 36
(pre-push network, expected), **`write_temporary_checkpoint` 28** (the redaction
path — these are pre-#2002, so re-check), **`process_sessions` 27** (post-commit
condensation), `prepare_and_validate_transcript` 2, `redact_transcript` 2. Collect
a few days of post-#2002 data and read `grep '"slow":true'` again.

## Known-but-unfixed

- **`process_sessions` (post-commit condensation)** is dominant in 27 slow traces,
  confirming what `docs/architecture/commit-hook-perf-analysis.md` documented
  independently: ~73-103ms per accumulated session, N sessions per commit. Never
  addressed.
- **The dead transcript sentinel: fixed ~520ms per Stop.** Diagnosed, never fixed
  — see [[claude-code-has-no-flush-sentinel]]. Was ~15% of the 3.4s p50.
- **Prefix reuse covers only the shadow write.** Condensation
  (`manual_commit_condensation.go`) and the Stop finalize rewrite
  (`manual_commit_hooks.go`) still redact whole transcripts; they inherit the
  sharding but not the reuse, so a mid-turn-commit Stop and every user commit still
  pay a full pass. Stated as a scope limit in #2002 rather than implied.
- **Upstream:** `cancelreader`'s epoll path reads `File.Fd()` after `Close()`, and
  bubbletea's `shutdown(kill=true)` leaves that reader unjoined with no API to
  await it. Not reported to charmbracelet.

---
name: ci-race-in-login-tty
description: "How to read the CI failure where ~30 unrelated cli tests fail at once — it's one -race report, not a panic"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 494613eb-2fb9-404c-b7b6-587999007d63
  modified: 2026-08-14T19:51:13.562Z
---

Diagnosed 2026-08-14, fixed in PR #2006.

**Symptom that misleads:** `test` / `test-core` fail with ~30 unrelated failures in
`cmd/entire/cli` at once (`TestMergeUnique`, `TestActivityModel_ScrollKeys`,
`TestBuildRepoDir`, …). That breadth is not systemic breakage and usually not your
change — one failure kills the test binary and Go reports every test in the package
as failed.

**It was a data race, not a panic.** `grep "panic:"` over `gh run view --log-failed`
finds nothing, because the real marker is `WARNING: DATA RACE`. Only the `-race`
jobs (`test`, `test-core`) catch it; `test-integration`, canary, and Windows all
pass, which is itself a hint. Grep for `DATA RACE` and read the two stacks.

**The bug:** `readLoginURLActionFromTTY` (`login.go`) closed its TTY with an
unconditional `defer`. Bubble Tea's `shutdown(kill bool)` only joins the input
reader when `!kill`, and context cancellation takes `shutdown(true)` — so
`ultraviolet.TerminalReader.StreamEvents` can still run after `Run()` returns. On
Linux that reader is `cancelreader`'s epoll implementation, whose wait loop reads
`tty.Fd()`, racing `poll.(*FD).destroy()`. macOS uses a different cancelreader that
never touches `Fd()`, so it **never reproduces locally** — CI on Linux is the only
verification.

**`Program.Wait()` is a trap here.** It looks like the way to join the reader but
waits on `p.finished`, which `Run()` closes via its own `defer` — so it returns
immediately, and on the one early return where `p.finished` is still nil it would
block forever. There is no API to await that goroutine; the fix is to not reclaim
the descriptor on the cancelled path.

**How to apply:** when a Go package reports many unrelated test failures in CI but
passes locally, (1) grep the log for `DATA RACE` before `panic`, (2) check whether
only the `-race` jobs failed, and (3) suspect platform-specific code paths before
suspecting your own diff — and don't call it a flake on one green run. See
[[hook-benchmark-methodology]] for the related trap of trusting a single sample.

skills.name: simplify
skills.content:
`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

=== cursor[bot] — cmd/entire/cli/trace_cmd.go:78 === ### Slow filter ignores last window **Medium Severity** `--slow` is applied after `collectTraceEntries` already truncated to `--last`, while `--hook` is applied before that truncation. With DEBUG traces present, `--last N --slow` keeps slow rows only among the last N traces rather than the last N slow ones, so `--summary --slow` and plain `--slow` can look empty and fall through to the “no traces / how to enable” message even when older slow entries exist in the log.
Additional Locations (1) - [`cmd/entire/cli/trace.go#L234-L247`](https://github.com/entireio/cli/blob/2b35da67573c28998c664c5afda56a5772f65b4e/cmd/entire/cli/trace.go#L234-L247)
 
Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 2b35da67573c28998c664c5afda56a5772f65b4e. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot). === Copilot — cmd/entire/cli/trace.go:489 === percentileMs() claims to use the nearest-rank percentile, but the current index calculation uses floor division. Trail: feat(doctor): aggregate hook traces, and correct the trace help text
  Number:  1118
  ID:      01M0HQF8VB6S01E8Z093M6WFQZ
  Branch:  soph/doctor-trace-aggregate
  Base:    main
  Status:  open
  Author:  Soph
  Phase:   building
  URL:     https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1118
  Assignees: Soph
  Type:      task
  Created: 2026-08-21T08:37:18Z
  Updated: 2026-08-21T08:37:18Z

Description:
Problem:
The entire doctor trace command shows individual hook invocations, but when there are many slow traces recorded over time, users can't easily see patterns—which steps consistently consume time, or how busy a particular hook is overall.
Solution:
Add an aggregation view to the trace command that rolls up many invocations into summary statistics. New flags:
--summary shows per-hook counts, slow counts, and percentiles (p50, p90, max), plus a list of steps ranked by total time consumed
--slow filters to only slow traces (those logged at WARN level)
--json outputs raw trace entries as JSON for scripting
The summary defaults to the last 200 traces (not just 1) when --last is not given, since aggregating a single trace is not useful.

Description:
Problem:
The entire doctor trace command shows individual hook invocations, but when there are many slow traces recorded over time, users can't easily see patterns—which steps consistently consume time, or how busy a particular hook is overall.
Solution:
Add an aggregation view to the trace command that rolls up many invocations into summary statistics. New flags:
--summary shows per-hook counts, slow counts, and percentiles (p50, p90, max), plus a list of steps ranked by total time consumed
--slow filters to only slow traces (those logged at WARN level)
--json outputs raw trace entries as JSON for scripting
The summary defaults to the last 200 traces (not just 1) when --last is not given, since aggregating a single trace is not useful.

Here's what came back.

## Entire trail 1118: no findings

The `Entire Gates` failure is just the **missing approval** — `entire trail approvals 1118` → "No approvals on trail #1118". No findings at any severity, including dismissed and stale. That gate is yours to clear.

Worth noting: my first `entire trail finding list` ran against *this* worktree's branch, not the PR's, so its "No findings" was meaningless. The `--trail 1118` query is the one that counts.

## The bots found four things, and three were real

I fixed all four (pushed as `ec5a11609`):

**`--slow` was applied after `--last` had already truncated** (Cursor, Medium — correct). `--hook` filters during the scan; `--slow` filtered the survivors. So `--last N --slow` meant "slow traces among the last N," not "the last N slow traces." This is currently invisible because every recorded trace is slow — but it breaks precisely when someone follows *this command's own advice* and sets `ENTIRE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`: fast traces fill the window and `--slow` reports "no traces" over a log holding hundreds. Both filters now run before truncation.

**`percentileMs` truncated the rank where its doc comment promised nearest-rank** (Copilot — correct). Overshot by a full sample whenever `p*n` divided evenly, so p90 of 10 samples returned the max, making P90 and MAX duplicate columns. Worth knowing for the numbers I gave you earlier: at n=38 and n=27 the old math happened to agree, but the `stop` row's p50 (n=32) was one sample high.

**The `Long` text hardcoded `1.5s` and `ENTIRE_PERF_SLOW_MS`** (Copilot — correct, and the sharpest of the four). The empty-state renderer prints both from `perf` constants; I left a hardcoded copy three lines away. That duplication is *exactly* what let this help text go stale in the first place, so fixing the text without fixing the pattern would have re-armed the same bug. Now formatted from the constants.

**`--json` emitted a year-1 timestamp** (Copilot — real but marginal). Only reachable via a missing/malformed `time` key, which the parser deliberately tolerates. `omitzero` was one word.

**One thing the bots missed**, which real data surfaced: the summary padded durations as numbers against string-width headers, so every column drifted a character once a 5-digit duration appeared — my `12471ms` pre-push rows were visibly crooked. Durations are now padded as strings, sharing one width with the header.

Verification: 3 new regression tests (the filter-ordering property, nearest-rank at the round-numbered cases, absent-vs-zero time), `lint` 0 issues, `test:ci` green — 56 vogon + 4 roger-roger canary, no failures. I have a monitor on CI and will report when it lands.

I have not replied to the bot comments — say the word if you want that.

content.content:
---
name: trail-write-gotchas
description: "entire trail write gotchas: the body has its own PUT route (the old PATCH 503 was a wrong-route bug), labels are not writable, and probing safely needs a scratch trail with a branch"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Gotchas when exercising `entire trail` **writes** against entire-api.

There is no backend switch to set: `ENTIRE_TRAILS_BACKEND` was removed on
2026-08-18 and entire-api is the only backend, so writes work by default. (The
old advice to export that var is dead — don't go looking for it.)

- **A trail's description is written by `PUT .../trails/{host}/{owner}/{repo}/{number}/body`, never by the trail PATCH.**
  The PATCH route answers a `body` field with an unconditional 503, and the API
  redacts 5xx messages, so the caller sees a bare "Service Unavailable" — which
  is why the earlier probe (2026-08-17, trail #1017, 200 B–4 KB, retried over
  ~10 minutes) read as a flaky server or a size limit. It was neither: wrong
  route. Fixed in the CLI on 2026-08-19 (`sendTrailBody` in `trail_cmd.go`);
  `api.TrailUpdateRequest` deliberately has no `Body` field so the mistake
  cannot be re-made. The PUT takes `{markdown, overwrite}` (or `contentJson`
  instead of `markdown`) and **refuses a non-empty description with 409
  `document_not_empty` unless `overwrite: true`** — that flag is what makes
  editing an existing description work at all. Its `If-Match` alternative is
  unusable from a read: the ETag comes only from this route's own response
  header, and `bodyDocument.updatedAt` from a trail read is formatted to a
  different precision, so a reconstructed header never matches.
- **Labels are read-only.** `--add-label`/`--remove-label` no longer exist; the
  API accepts no label writes. Reads (`trail show`'s `Labels:` line) still work.
- **Probing safely needs a scratch trail *with* a branch.** `trail update` can
  only target a trail **by branch**, so a `--no-branch` scratch trail is
  unpatchable — but creating one with `--branch` also **creates and pushes that
  branch to origin**. Clean up both the trail and the remote branch afterwards.

Related: [[trail-tune-command]], [[no-fluff-in-review-artifacts]]

input.content:
---
name: trail-finding-read-defaults
description: "entire trail finding list silently answers for the CURRENT branch with narrow filters — 'No findings found' is not evidence a PR has no findings"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Hit 2026-08-21 while checking PR #2092's findings from a worktree parked on an
unrelated branch.

`entire trail finding list` with no arguments resolves the **current branch's**
trail, and defaults to `--status open --freshness current`. Both failure modes
are silent — you get `No findings found.` rather than an error — so the wrong
branch and the right branch are indistinguishable in the output.

To read another PR's findings, pin the trail and widen the filters:

```
entire trail finding list --trail <number> --status any --freshness any --include-dismissed
```

Get the number from the `Entire Gates` check's `detailsUrl`
(`…/trails/<number>`), or `entire trail list --status any`. `entire trail show
<number>` confirms which branch it belongs to — check that the `Branch:` line
matches the PR before believing a finding count.

**Also:** a failing `Entire Gates` check does **not** imply findings. A trail
with zero findings still fails the gate on a missing approval; confirm with
`entire trail approvals <number>` before hunting for code problems.

Note `--trail` is a flag on `trail finding` (inherited by `list`), while `trail
show` takes the selector **positionally** — `trail show --trail N` prints root
usage and exits, which reads like an unrelated CLI error.

Related: [[trail-write-gotchas]], [[ask-before-posting-comments]]

Slow root perf spans log at WARN since #1984, so this no longer needs a bespoke harness.

```bash
import sys,json,collections
c=collections.Counter()

    d=json.loads(l)
    s={k[6:-3]:v for k,v in d.items() if k.startswith('steps.') and k.endswith('_ms')}
    if s: c[max(s,key=s.get)]+=1

```

That one-liner is a stand-in for a gap: `doctor trace` can show the last N traces but cannot
aggregate them, and has no `--json`, which the repo's agent-safe CLI convention would expect.

  user pays that, and it silently dominates any measurement taken here.
- **`git clone` does not copy `refs/entire/*`.** A clone has no checkpoint history, so it
  cannot reproduce costs that scale with accumulated sessions. Copy the repo instead.

content.text:
Yes, with two things deliberately left open and one that isn't mine to do.

**Shipped and merged — five PRs:** #1984 (WARN slow spans), #1985 (shared object cache), #2002 (sharded + incremental redaction), #2006 (login TTY race), #2092 (trace aggregation + help text). Worktree is clean, nothing unpushed.

**Two follow-ups I owed, now done:**

- #2091 still handed you that grep+python one-liner for a gap #2092 closed. It now says `entire doctor trace --summary --slow --last 500`, with two caveats I'd otherwise have lost: the command reads *one* repo's log (so a cross-repo sweep still needs the grep), and its dominance is time-weighted while the old one-liner counted — so any ranking from the old method has to be re-derived, not carried forward. That's the same defect the bots and I hit in the summary code itself.
- Memory updated to match, and the pre-#2002 step ranking is now explicitly labelled as counted-and-soft rather than sitting there looking authoritative.

**Left open on purpose, tracked in [#2091](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/2091):** the actual perf question. The ~3s p50 floor is still unexplained, `process_sessions` is untouched, the dead sentinel's ~520ms is still paid, and prefix reuse still only covers the shadow write. Post-#2002 data was n=4 when I filed it — Tuesday's re-measure is the point.

**Not done:** the upstream `cancelreader`/`Fd()`-after-`Close()` report to charmbracelet. It's recorded as a loose end in #2091.

**Not mine to touch:** branch cleanup. The five session branches are all merged, but so are ~350 others repo-wide, and this worktree is currently sitting on `soph/doctor-trace-aggregate` — deleting it would change your working state. Say the word and I'll clean just the five.

content.text:
Yes — worth doing, and it's easier than I thought, but **not in the repo I named**. That part of #2091 was pointing at the wrong project.

## The fix belongs in `charmbracelet/ultraviolet`

Charm has re-implemented cancelreader *inside* ultraviolet (`poll_linux.go`, `poll_bsd.go`, `poll_select.go`), and the bug came across verbatim:

- `poll_linux.go:123` — `case int32(r.file.Fd()):` after `EpollWait` returns
- `poll_bsd.go:113` — `case uint64(r.file.Fd()):` after `Kevent` returns

Both read `Fd()` on the caller's file *after* the blocking wake — exactly the window a cancel opens. `muesli/cancelreader` has the identical lines, but sending a PR there is pointless: **last substantive merge June 2022**, and 7 open PRs spanning 2022–2026, none merged.

## Their policies: unusually easy

No CLA, no DCO, no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in either bubbletea or ultraviolet (checked root and `.github` — just issue templates, dependabot, workflows). MIT. Conventional-commit titles are the house style. No issue-first requirement in evidence: **8 of bubbletea's last 14 merged PRs came from forks**, several from first-time contributors, merged within days. Ultraviolet does the same (#150, fork, merged next day). Nothing upstream reports this yet — I searched race/Fd/DATA RACE/waitForReadLoop in all three repos.

## The easy half is also the effective half

Cache the two fds as ints at construction — they're already computed there for `EpollCtl`/`SetKevent` — and compare the cached values. Two files, ~8 lines, no API or behaviour change. It has an argument beyond the race, too: `os.File.Fd()` pulls the descriptor out of the runtime poller, so calling it on every wake is undesirable regardless.

And it's *sufficient* — the racing access was `Fd()` itself, so removing it kills the race. `file.Read()` on a closed file is properly synchronized.

The bubbletea half is the hard one and I'd keep it separate: `shutdown(kill=true)` deliberately skips `waitForReadLoop()`, and there's no API to await the reader, so "when may a caller reclaim the fd it passed in?" is a semantics question for the maintainers. That's an issue, not a drive-by PR.

## A correction I owe you

I told you macOS "uses a different cancelreader that never touches `Fd()`." Wrong mechanism — every implementation calls it. The real reason, now verified: `poll_select.go` calls `Fd()` *before* blocking in `select` and compares captured ints afterward, while epoll calls it *after* the wake. And our TTY takes the select path on darwin only because both libraries special-case it — `if file.Name() == "/dev/tty"` → select, with the comment *"kqueue returns instantly when polling /dev/tty"*. So "Linux-only, CI is the only verification" still holds; my explanation for it didn't. Memory corrected.

Want me to open the ultraviolet PR? I'd send the fd-caching fix for both pollers with a race-reproducing test, and file the bubbletea shutdown question as a separate issue — but both are outward-facing under your name, so I'll wait for your go-ahead.

content.text:
They shouldn't wait — 0.10.2 is already collecting the data we need.

## They can report usefully today

The key fact: **#1984 shipped in 0.10.2** (merged 08-14, release cut 08-19). So slow hook traces log at **WARN**, and the default level is INFO — meaning with *zero configuration* their `.entire/logs/entire.log` already contains a step-by-step breakdown of every hook that took ≥1.5s. Nothing to enable, nothing to reproduce.

So the best single action is:

```
entire doctor bundle
```

It's been in since April, so it's in their build. It zips `.entire/logs/`, settings, `git status`/`log`/`remote`, and a `version.txt` — **and redacts secrets by default** (`--raw` is opt-in), which matters because the bug template currently just says "review output for sensitive information before posting." Attach that to a [bug report](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/new?template=bug_report.yml); general questions go to the Discord in `config.yml`.

If they want to look themselves, `entire doctor trace --last 20` works in 0.10.2. Only `--summary`/`--slow`/`--json` are missing — those merged today, *after* today's nightly was cut at 06:13, so they land in tomorrow's.

## On upgrading — depends how the issue reads

If it's the hook slowness we've been chasing, **#2002 is not in 0.10.2** but is in today's nightly:

```
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly
```

Two honest caveats. #2002 rewrites transcript redaction on the checkpoint-write path — that's the highest-value fix but not a cosmetic one, and nightly is a pre-release. And stable cadence here is fast (0.10.1 on 08-18, 0.10.2 on 08-19), so 0.10.3 is probably days away. For a user who isn't blocked, waiting for stable is reasonable; for one who's actively suffering slow hooks, the nightly is the fix.

**Ask them to send the bundle before upgrading, though.** Once they're on the nightly, the pre-fix evidence is gone — and post-#2002 data is exactly what's thin in #2091 (n=4 when I filed it). Their bundle is worth more to us than to them.

One gap worth fixing on our side: the bug template asks people to hand-paste from `.entire/logs/` and never mentions `entire doctor bundle`, so reporters do the redaction work themselves and usually send less than we need. Want me to open a PR adding it to the template?

Investigated 2026-08-21. The upstream half of the [[ci-race-in-login-tty]] bug that
#2006 worked around locally. Not yet reported.

## The target is ultraviolet, not cancelreader

Charm re-implemented `muesli/cancelreader` inside `charmbracelet/ultraviolet`
(`poll_linux.go`, `poll_bsd.go`, `poll_select.go`, `poll_fallback.go`), and the
defect came across verbatim. At `ultraviolet@v0.0.0-20260811164956`:

- `poll_linux.go:123` — `case int32(r.file.Fd()):` evaluated *after* `EpollWait`
  returns
- `poll_bsd.go:113` — `case uint64(r.file.Fd()):` after `Kevent` returns

`bubbletea/v2` (module path `charm.land/bubbletea/v2`) still imports
`muesli/cancelreader` in `tea.go` for the `CancelReader` type, so `go mod why`
points at the dead repo and is misleading about which code runs.

**Don't send a PR to `muesli/cancelreader`.** Last substantive merge 2022-06-22,
last push 2023-07, 7 open PRs spanning 2022–2026 with none merged.

## Why it's Linux-only, precisely

Every implementation calls `Fd()`; what differs is *when* relative to the block:

- epoll and kqueue call it **after** the wake → races a concurrent `Close()`.
- `poll_select.go` captures `readerFd`/`abortFd` **before** `unix.Select` and
  compares the captured ints afterward → no post-wake access.
- On darwin our TTY takes the select path only because both libraries special-case
  it: `if file.Name() == "/dev/tty"` → `newSelectPollReader`, commented "kqueue
  returns instantly when polling /dev/tty". So a BSD reader on any *other* file is
  vulnerable.

## The fix

Cache the two fds as ints in the reader struct at construction — `newPollReader`
already computes them for `EpollCtl`/`SetKevent` — and compare the cached values.
Two files, ~8 lines, no API or behaviour change. Second argument for it:
`os.File.Fd()` pulls the descriptor out of the runtime poller, so calling it on
every wake is undesirable regardless of the race. This alone kills our race, since
the racing access *was* `Fd()`; `file.Read()` on a closed file is synchronized.

The bubbletea half is separate and harder: `shutdown(kill=true)` skips
`waitForReadLoop()` and exposes no API to await the reader, so a caller has no safe
moment to reclaim a `*os.File` it passed in. That's a semantics change needing
maintainer buy-in — file an issue, not a PR. `Program.Wait()` is not the answer
(see [[ci-race-in-login-tty]]).

## Charm's contribution policy (checked 2026-08-21)

Unusually low-friction: **no CLA, no DCO, no CONTRIBUTING.md** in bubbletea or
ultraviolet (root and `.github` — only issue templates, dependabot, workflows).
MIT. Conventional-commit titles are the house style (`fix:`, `fix(key):`,
`feat:`). No issue-first requirement in evidence: 8 of bubbletea's last 14 merged
PRs came from forks, several by first-time contributors, merged within days;
ultraviolet does the same. No existing upstream issue/PR for this (searched race,
Fd, DATA RACE, waitForReadLoop across all three repos).

content.text:
I was wrong, and it's worth spelling out because it unblocks the re-measure.

## What the constraint was

It came from you on 08-13: measure in a repo that isn't this one, because this one pays for compiled hooks. The mechanism was real — this repo's hooks were wired to `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher that `go build`/`go run`'d the CLI from the working tree on *every* hook invocation, ~1.53 s of pure toolchain cost per hook. No user and no other repo paid it, and it silently swamped whatever you were trying to measure. That's precisely what made me mis-rank findings early on.

## It stopped being true on 08-17

**#1999 removed `local_dev` mode entirely.** `scripts/entire-dev` is deleted, and hooks now name the plain binary. This repo's `.claude/settings.json`:

```
Stop: sh -c '... exec entire hooks claude-code stop'
```

`which entire` → `/Users/soph/.local/bin/entire`, running `0.10.3-nightly...`. A real released build. The only surviving `entire-dev` strings are drift-detection patterns at `hook_command.go:117-118`, kept so `doctor` can flag the legacy config.

So hook timings taken here today **are** product timings. My reason for saying the re-measure was blocked was stale — #1999 landed mid-investigation, four days before I restated the constraint, and I never rechecked the premise. It also means the numbers I showed you on 08-21 from this worktree were legitimate; I hedged them for no reason.

## What actually still holds

1. **Interleave A/B runs.** This is the one that bit hardest — sequential runs gave #1985 a fake 49% win from page-cache warming; interleaved after warmup it was 2%.
2. **Don't measure a fresh clone.** `git clone` doesn't copy `refs/entire/*`, so a clone has no checkpoint history and can't reproduce anything that scales with accumulated sessions. Copy the repo.
3. **Don't generalize from one repo** — which I think was the real substance of your instruction. Session size, checkpoint count, and agent drive these numbers more than the code does, so a user-reported problem gets characterized where the user is.

That third point is a caution about inference, not a prohibition on measuring.

Three records still carry the dead version — `docs/architecture/commit-hook-perf-analysis.md:172`, issue #2091 line 92, and my methodology memory. Want me to correct all three? And since the constraint's gone, I can run the post-#2002 re-measure here now.

    tot=collections.Counter()
    for x in g: tot[x[4]]+=x[5]

    print("  dominant steps by TOTAL time:")
    for s,ms in tot.most_common(8):

    print("  by op:")
    ops=collections.defaultdict(list)

        print(f"    {op:20} n={len(v):3}  p50={pct(v,50):6.0f}ms  max={max(v):6.0f}ms")

Stefan's rule (2026-08-13): **benchmark hooks in a repo that is not the CLI repo,
with a compiled binary.**

**Why:** the CLI repo pays ~1.53 s per hook for `scripts/entire-dev`
(`go build` probe + `go run`) that no other repo and no user ever pays, and it has
an atypical 1.5 GB object store. Measuring there makes dev tooling look like
product cost and misranks every real finding. Users report hook latency with a
released binary in an ordinary repo — measure that.

**How to apply:**
- Clone a real non-CLI repo locally (`git clone --local <src> <tmp>`), run
  `entire enable` in the *clone*, never the source. Vary repo size — flat timings
  across a wide pack-size range are strong evidence a cost is fixed, not I/O.
- Drive hooks directly: `echo '<payload>' | ENTIRE_TEST_CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR=<td>
  <binary> hooks claude-code <hook>`. Isolate `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR`,
  `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE`.
- Get the per-step breakdown from `{"log_level":"DEBUG"}` in
  `.entire/settings.local.json`, then diff consecutive log timestamps.

**Two traps that each produced a wrong answer here:**
1. **Sequential A/B is invalid** — running variant A's runs then variant B's let
   the OS page cache warm across the boundary and showed a fake 49% win for the
   shared object cache. Interleaved with warmup it was 2%. Always warm both
   binaries first, then alternate A/B/A/B and report medians.
2. **A synthetic microbenchmark can invert the ranking** — re-reading 733 blobs of
   one tree predicted ~4× from the object-cache fix; the real hook access pattern
   is page-cache-warm and got 2%. Validate a mechanism against the live hook
   before believing its magnitude.

content.text:
Yes — precisely. And importantly it's the scope limit #2002 **documented**, not the bug #2002 fixed. His diagnosis is correct, including the fix he proposes.

## Why it fits

`manual_commit_hooks.go:2921` — the Stop finalize rewrite calls `redact.JSONLBytes(fullTranscript)` directly, with no cache threaded in. #2002 shipped *two* mechanisms, and only one reaches here:

- **Sharding** (parallel per-line pass) → applies everywhere, including this path.
- **Prefix reuse** (redact only appended lines) → only where a cache is passed, i.e. the shadow write via `createRedactedBlobFromFile`.

So this path still redacts from byte zero every Stop. His phrasing — "rewrote the full transcript into the checkpoint", "make stop-time finalization incremental" — names that exact path. It's independent confirmation of #2091 item 4.

His post-commit number is the same story: 28.6s "on redaction alone" is condensation, i.e. `process_sessions`, also uncovered by reuse. That's #2091 item 2 — which yesterday's re-measure had just promoted to the top actionable cost (29.6% of slow-trace time).

**Codex is where this bites first.** Its transcripts carry base64 encrypted-reasoning payloads, the pathological input for the entropy layer — which is exactly why sanitize-before-redact is load-bearing in that pipeline. 65 MB of Codex rollout is the worst case in the codebase.

## One number tells you which build he's on

28.6s on ~65 MB versus my pre-fix measurement of 66.7s on 70 MB — roughly 2.4× faster per byte, which is about what sharding across cores buys. That's **consistent with him having #2002 and hitting the uncovered path**, not with him missing #2002 entirely.

I want to be clear that's an inference, not a fact — core count and disk differ, and it changes the advice completely. If he's pre-#2002, upgrading may just fix it. If post, it needs new work. `entire version` settles it in one line.

And the data already exists without reproducing: #1984 shipped in **0.10.2**, so if he's on that or later, his `.entire/logs/entire.log` already holds WARN traces with the step breakdown. `entire doctor bundle` collects it, redacted by default.

## Warn him about the workaround

Raising the Stop timeout works but **gets silently reverted**. `dropStaleEntireHooks` treats an Entire hook whose command matches but whose timeout differs as *stale* — it deletes the entry and re-adds it at `defaultHookTimeoutSec = 30`. On top of that, `doctor` reports hook-config drift and prompts `entire enable --force`, which would undo it. So it's fine as a stopgap, but he shouldn't count on it surviving.

On damage: consistent with his read that commit and push succeeded. An incomplete condense leaves `FullyCondensed` false and PostCommit retries, so it's fail-open by design rather than lost data.

## What this changes

It escalates #2091 item 4 from a latency footnote to user-visible breakage — a hook being *killed*, not just slow. Combined with yesterday's finding that the compact transcript is also generated twice per Stop (`persistent.go:1092` and `:2069`, 904ms of a 2505ms Stop), the Stop path now has two independent whole-session passes that should be incremental.

Want me to add his report to #2091 and start on extending prefix reuse to the finalize and condensation paths? That's the fix he's asking for, and it's the same mechanism already proven in `redact_cache.go`.

those functions no longer exist. Nothing in cmd/ initializes logging that way

A semantic merge conflict — the kind where both sides are individually green:

- **#1877** added a `logging.Debug` call to `deleteTempFiles`, plus the `logging` import.
- **#2002** independently rewrote `clean.go`'s import block (the redaction-cache section).

Stopping here to flag this, because it outranks the feature work.

## `origin/main` does not compile — [PR #2105](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2105) fixes it

```
$ go build ./...
cmd/entire/cli/clean.go:485:4: undefined: logging
```

I reproduced it on a **pristine detached worktree at `origin/main` (fe80c26d2)**, so it isn't local state.

**A semantic merge conflict — both sides were individually green.** #1877 added a `logging.Debug` call to `deleteTempFiles` along with the import; my #2002 independently rewrote `clean.go`'s import block for the redaction-cache section. The merge took the *import block from main* and the *Debug call from the branch*. Per-PR CI compiled each branch; nothing built the merge result.

**Good news on releases:** the break is in fe80c26d2 only. Today's nightly (`...202608230611.b1e086253`) was cut from the **parent**, so nothing published carries it — but the next nightly build would have failed.

**One thing I got wrong and the compiler caught.** The merge also dropped a `logging.SetLogLevelGetter` / `logging.Init` / `defer logging.Close()` block from #1877's branch, and I read that as more lost work and restored it. All three symbols are gone — nothing in `cmd/` initializes logging that way any more, since the package-level helpers resolve through `LoggerFromContext` with a `slog.Default()` fallback. So the merge's *outcome* was right for the current API and only the import was missing. Import-only is the fix; I'd have shipped a worse one on instinct.

Verified: `go build ./...` clean, lint 0 issues, `go vet` clean, `cli` tests pass.

## Your feature work is stashed, not lost

On `soph/incremental-finalize-redaction` (off main) I'd already built the foundation before hitting this:

- Parameterized `redactIncrementally` by a **redactor function**, used for both the appended suffix *and* the whole-content fallback — so a prefix from one pipeline can never be spliced onto a suffix from another.
- Added `TranscriptScope` namespacing. This turned out to be necessary, not decorative: the shadow write redacts **sanitized** bytes, while condensation and finalize redact **sanitized + image-externalized** bytes. One shared key would have been safe (the hash check rejects mismatches) but would have missed on every single checkpoint.
- Added exported `RedactTranscriptIncremental` for the two in-memory paths, keyed per session so concurrent sessions can't share an entry.

Still to do: wire the two call sites (`manual_commit_hooks.go:2921` and `redactSessionTranscript`) and write the tests — including the property that matters most, that incremental output is byte-identical to a whole-transcript pass.

Want me to carry on with that now on top of the fix branch, or hold until #2105 lands?

content.content: 745:  - The checkpoint metadata walk reuses the previous checkpoint's redacted blob as a prefix and redacts only appended lines (`checkpoint/redact_cache.go`), turning a per-Stop cost of O(whole transcript) into O(appended). The stored prefix must always end immediately after a `\n`, which is what makes plain byte concatenation reproduce the full result; content with a partial trailing line is therefore never cached. Eligibility is keyed on `paths.TranscriptFileName` (`full.jsonl`), **not** a `.jsonl` suffix — `transcript.jsonl` is regenerated in full each checkpoint and `full.jsonl.001` chunks are not appended, so neither should qualify. Reuse requires the prefix bytes to still hash the same and `redactionFingerprint()` (CLI version + commit + `redact.ConfigFingerprint()`) to match, so a rewritten transcript, changed custom rules, or a CLI upgrade all fall back to a full redaction. Bump `configFingerprintVersion` in `redact/fingerprint.go` whenever the regex layers change behaviour, or stale output can be reused. The cache lives in the git common dir (via the memoized `resolveGitCommonDir`), never under `.entire/`, because anything in the metadata directory would be walked into the checkpoint tree and committed. Only the shadow write is covered: condensation and the Stop finalize rewrite still redact whole transcripts, inheriting the sharding but not the prefix reuse.

## What it does

Closes the scope limit #2002 shipped with. Both remaining whole-transcript paths — post-commit condensation and the Stop finalize rewrite — now reuse the prefix redacted for the previous checkpoint through a new `checkpoint.RedactTranscriptIncremental`.

## Two things that turned out to be about correctness, not speed

**The redactor is now a parameter, used for both the suffix and the whole-content fallback.** Before, the suffix was hardcoded to `RedactBlobBytes` while each caller picked its own fallback — so the two could diverge and splice a prefix from one pipeline onto a suffix from another. I'd initially have shared one key. That would have been **safe** — the prefix hash rejects a mismatch — but it would have missed on every single checkpoint. A silently useless cache, which is harder to notice than a broken one.

## The test I'd want a reviewer to look at

Byte-identity across five appends is the core property. But on its own **that test passes just as happily with the cache doing nothing** — so there's a second one that counts the bytes handed to the redactor and asserts it sees only the appended suffix. Without it the suite would have been decorative.

Also covered: scope and session isolation, error propagation on both the full *and* suffix paths (a degraded scanner must fail the write, never ship a reused prefix alone), and OpenCode's single-JSON-value shape never being cached for splicing.

## Two notes on the diff

- `redactFinalizedTranscript` is extracted because eight added lines pushed `finalizeAllTurnCheckpoints` past `maintidx`. Extraction was the honest fix; a `nolint` wasn't.
- The per-subagent transcript opts out with a nil repo — written once per task, never appended across checkpoints, so there's nothing to reuse.

Review target: `2107`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

There are now TWO entry points into the same cache: `createRedactedBlobFromFile` (file-walking, passes a *redactCache it received) and the new exported `RedactTranscriptIncremental` (in-memory, resolves its own cache via repoRedactCache). Is that the right factoring, or is one the general case and the other a special case that should be expressed in terms of it? All four review agents are running in parallel — reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude.

While they work, here's the scope they're looking at:

| File | Δ |
|---|---|
| `checkpoint/redact_cache.go` | +117 |
| `checkpoint/redact_cache_scope_test.go` | +212 (new) |
| `strategy/manual_commit_hooks.go` | +67 |
| `strategy/manual_commit_condensation.go` | +26 |
| `checkpoint/redact_cache_test.go` | +14 |
| `checkpoint/persistent.go` | +5 |
| `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/…perf-analysis.md` | +11 |

I've pointed each agent at the specific things I'm least sure about rather than letting them roam, since I wrote this code and know where the soft spots are:

- **Reuse** — whether `RedactTranscriptIncremental` duplicates the load→fallback→blob→store dance already in `createRedactedBlobFromFile`, and whether `redactFinalizedTranscript` and `redactOrDrop` have converged enough to share.
- **Simplification** — the `full` closure that adapts the redactor but may be redundant against the direct fallback call, and the `counting` closure repeated across three tests.
- **Efficiency** — the one I most expect to bite: `RedactTranscriptIncremental` calls `CreateBlobFromContent` purely to get a hash for the cache, and the store writes the same bytes again. On a 65MB transcript that's worth knowing whether git dedups or whether I've added a second write to the exact path I'm trying to speed up.
- **Altitude** — the synthetic tree path. The in-memory callers have no real tree path, so `transcriptCacheKey` fabricates one ending in `full.jsonl` purely to satisfy `incrementalRedactionCandidate`'s filename gate. That's encoding a policy decision in a synthetic string, and I want a second opinion on whether the deeper fix is to make eligibility explicit instead.

I'll report what they find and apply the fixes once all four are back.

`redactIncrementally` (`redact_cache.go:221-300`) remains the single general core and both entry points are thin adapters over it; injecting `transcriptRedactor` instead of the hardcoded `RedactBlobBytes` call is the correct generalization and is what makes the pipeline the caller's business. Three in, and they converge tightly. Reuse independently found the fix I'd guessed at, and it's better than I realized:

**Route finalize through `redactSessionTranscript` — the same-package function it duplicates.** That single change collapses four separate findings: it deletes the duplicated span+call body, it makes both committed callers share *one* redactor (`redactSessionJSONLBytes`), which structurally eliminates altitude's divergent-pipeline hazard, it lets the two existing seam tests reach finalize for the first time, and finalize gains the duration logging it currently lacks.

**And that dissolves the scope abstraction rather than justifying it.** Once both in-memory callers go through one function with one pipeline, `TranscriptScope` has one production value and one pipeline behind it. So the honest resolution is: delete the enum, key on session ID, keep one sentence noting the shadow path keys on its real tree path (which is what actually prevents collision), and fix the CLAUDE.md claim. The tautological "scopes are isolated" test goes with it; the session-isolation test stays.

Reuse also caught two things I'd have missed: `openCodeExport(t, minBytes)` already exists in the sibling test file — I hand-rolled the same fixture ten lines away from it — and my two copies of the storePrefix protocol have *already* drifted, since `persistent.go` treats a blob-write error as fatal while my new code silently skips caching.

One thing I'm adopting beyond the findings: altitude's suggestion to attach `reused_bytes`/`redacted_bytes` to the `redact_transcript` perf span. Three lines, and it turns exactly the kind of silent cache degradation I just spent days unable to see into something `doctor trace --summary` surfaces.

Waiting on efficiency alone now — it owns the double-blob-write question that altitude and reuse both circled, so I'm not guessing at that one.

<result>## Findings (efficiency only, verified against code)

**1. `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/redact_cache.go:405-411` — the cache blob write is a genuine second full compression, not a free dedup; and for the PR's own 65MB example it is not deduped at all.**

Traced `CreateBlobFromContent` (`persistent.go:2411`) into go-git v6 (the pinned `v6.0.0-alpha.5.0.20260812155443`):
- `MemoryObject.Write` is `o.cont = append(o.cont, p...)` (`plumbing/memory.go:74`) → one 65MB alloc + memcpy.
- `ObjectStorage.SetEncodedObject` (`storage/filesystem/object.go:489`) has **no** pre-existence check: it opens a temp objfile writer and `CopyBufferPool`s the payload through `objfile.Writer`, which zlib-deflates while hashing (`plumbing/format/objfile/writer.go:82`), then returns `o.Hash()`, which hashes `o.cont` a **second** time (`plumbing/memory.go:28`).
- Dedup happens in `dotgit.ObjectWriter.save()` (`storage/filesystem/dotgit/writers.go:405-420`): `Lstat` the final path *after* the temp file is fully written, then `Remove` the temp. Dedup saves the rename, **not** the deflate. So the inline comment "git dedups it to the same object" is true about disk, false about CPU.

Cost per invocation over 65MB: 1×65MB copy, 2 full hash passes, 1 full zlib deflate (Go flate default on JSON ≈ 30-60 MB/s → **~1-2s CPU**), plus a ~10-20MB temp write + unlink. The store then deflates the same bytes again for its own blobs. This happens twice per commit-turn (condensation process at `manual_commit_condensation.go:854`, finalize process at `manual_commit_hooks.go:2839`). After this PR the redaction is O(appended) (tens of ms), so this duplicate write becomes a dominant share of what is left.

Worse at exactly 65MB: `agent.MaxChunkSize = 50MB` (`cmd/entire/cli/agent/chunking.go:16`), so the store writes **two chunk blobs**; the whole-transcript cache blob matches nothing → never deduped → a permanent unreachable ~65MB loose object per checkpoint (also prunable by `git gc`, after which every cache entry silently reverts to a full redaction; `entire clean` reclaims the JSON entries but not these blobs).

Cheaper alternatives, in order of preference:
- Mirror what the file path already does: `createRedactedBlobFromFile` (`persistent.go:2561-2568`) writes the blob **once** and hands that same hash to `storePrefix`. For finalize the hash already exists downstream — `PrecomputeTranscriptBlobs` (`persistent.go:2096-2111`) chunks the *unsanitized* `transcript.Bytes()`, so for a single chunk `ChunkHashes[0]` is bit-for-bit this hash. Record the prefix after the store write instead of before it. (`HasEncodedObject`-then-skip does not help, because the cache write is always the first one.)
- Or store the redacted prefix as a plain file in the cache dir (`RedactCacheDirName`, already outside `.entire/` and already `entire clean`-able): turns ~1-2s of deflate into a raw 65MB write, and removes the gc-prune fragility and the 2 hash passes.

**2. `redact_cache.go:290-292` — one avoidable full 65MB copy on every hit-path checkpoint.** `out := make([]byte, 0, len(prefix)+len(redactedSuffix)); append(out, prefix...)` copies the whole reused prefix, on top of the exact-size buffer `readBlobBytes` already allocated (`:321`). The line predates the diff, but the diff routes two more paths through it. Cheaper: redact the (small) suffix first, then read the blob into a buffer with `cap = blob.Size + len(redactedSuffix)` and append in place — saves 1 alloc + 1 memcpy of 65MB per checkpoint. Only downside: a blob-read failure after the suffix redaction wastes work proportional to the appended bytes only.

**3. `redact_cache.go:308-326` (`readBlobBytes`) — hit path now peaks around 5×transcript and thrashes the process-wide object cache, in two more processes.** go-git's `getFromUnpacked` (`storage/filesystem/object.go:715-765`) inflates the loose object into a `MemoryObject` and then does `s.objectCache.Put(obj)`. `LargeObjectThreshold` is not set (`cmd/entire/cli/gitrepo/repository.go:119-125`), and the LRU is the shared 96MB `cache.NewObjectLRUDefault()` (`repository.go:26`) — so a 65MB cached prefix evicts nearly everything else and is pinned for the process lifetime. Simultaneously live on a hit: source content + go-git MemoryObject + `readBlobBytes` buffer + joined `out` + `CreateBlobFromContent` MemoryObject ≈ **325MB** for a 65MB transcript. Cheaper: set `gitfilesystem.Options.LargeObjectThreshold` (e.g. 8MB) so big blobs stream and skip the LRU, or read the prefix from a plain cache file per 1(b), which removes the go-git copy and the LRU put outright.

**4. `repoRedactCache` per invocation — already cheap; one small ordering nit.** Verified `resolveGitCommonDir` memoizes process-wide keyed by worktree root (`git_common_dir.go:26-50`); only the first call per process forks `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` (~10ms). `newRedactCache`'s `os.MkdirAll` costs exactly 1 `stat` when the dir exists (stdlib returns after `Stat`) → ~µs, 2-3 per turn. Not worth changing. Nit: `RedactTranscriptIncremental` calls `repoRedactCache` (`:391`) *before* `redactIncrementally` checks `incrementalRedactionCandidate`, so a non-candidate payload (<1MiB, or a single-JSON OpenCode export) pays the resolution — and possibly that ~10ms fork, since in the post-commit process `redactOrDrop` runs before `getPersistentStore`/pushqueue — for nothing. blob, and the comment claiming git would dedup it was wrong about CPU. go-git
deflates the entire payload before dotgit discovers the object exists -- dedup
saves the rename, not the compression -- so a 65MB transcript paid ~1-2s of zlib

the store chunks transcripts at agent.MaxChunkSize (50MB), so above that the

clean` already reclaims. New test pins survival across `git gc --prune=all`.

Also: read the prefix into a buffer sized for prefix+suffix and join in place,
dropping a full copy of the reused prefix per checkpoint; and skip the
git-common-dir resolution for content that cannot use the cache anyway.

Reuse/altitude: redactFinalizedTranscript re-implemented redactSessionTranscript
from the same package, and the two shared a cache namespace while passing
*different* redactors -- condensation the injectable redactSessionJSONLBytes var,

bet on byte-identical output that nothing enforced, and the existing seam tests
could never reach finalize. Finalize now delegates, so one pipeline is structural.

two call sites that had already drifted (one treated a blob-write error as fatal,
the other skipped caching silently). Both callers lose their nil-check.

had a single production value, ShadowScope was referenced only by a test

content.text:
Applied and pushed to [#2107](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2107). Lint 0 issues, `test:ci` green (checkpoint 349s, strategy 112s, 56+4 canary).

## The finding that justified the whole exercise

**My "git dedups it to the same object" comment was wrong about CPU.** The efficiency agent traced it into go-git: `dotgit.ObjectWriter.save()` dedups by `Lstat`-ing the final path *after* the temp file is fully written. Dedup saves the rename, not the deflate.

So my cache-blob write cost ~1–2s of zlib per checkpoint on a 65MB transcript, on both new paths, purely to obtain a hash. And it's worse than slow: the store chunks at `MaxChunkSize = 50MB`, so above that my whole-transcript blob **matches no chunk, is never deduped, and leaves an unreachable ~65MB object per checkpoint** — which `git gc` then prunes, silently reverting the cache to full redaction. It also pinned 65MB in the shared 96MB go-git LRU.

I had added a measurable regression to the exact path this PR exists to speed up, with a comment asserting it was free. The prefix is now a plain file in the cache dir that `entire clean` already reclaims, and there's a test pinning survival across `git gc --prune=all`.

## Where the agents converged on something I'd argued for

**`redactFinalizedTranscript` re-implemented `redactSessionTranscript` from the same package** — and the two shared a cache namespace while passing *different* redactors: condensation the injectable `redactSessionJSONLBytes` var, finalize an inline closure. So my commit message's claim that divergence was "unrepresentable" was false twice over — and the existing seam tests could never reach finalize. It now delegates, making one pipeline structural.

The same fix **dissolved `TranscriptScope`**. Behind one function it had a single production value, `ShadowScope` was referenced only by a test asserting two keys differ, and my CLAUDE.md text called namespacing-by-scope the mechanism when the shadow write never passes a scope at all. That documentation error was the worst part — corrected, not restated.

Also moved the whole-content fallback inside `redactIncrementally`, where it belonged: the two hand-written copies had **already drifted** (one treated a blob-write error as fatal, the other skipped caching silently).

## Two skipped, deliberately

- **Perf-span `reused_bytes`/`redacted_bytes`.** I wanted this — it's exactly the cache-thrash signal I spent days lacking. But child-span attrs aren't serialized, so it needs a `perf` change outside this diff with its own tests. The Debug log already carries both numbers.
- **Deriving the key from pipeline identity** rather than caller. Right shape for a third in-memory pipeline; premature for one.

Net: +316/−228 across 7 files, and the mechanism is smaller than before the review despite doing more.

content.text:
Fixed and pushed. It wasn't a race or a failing assertion.

## `panic: test timed out after 10m0s`

The `checkpoint` package blew the deadline. I checked for `DATA RACE` first per my own notes from the last CI red — nothing; the marker was a plain timeout, with `TestIncrementalRedaction_SingleJSONValueNeverCached` merely being the test in flight when the alarm fired.

**Cause: `redactCacheMinBytes` gates prefix reuse at 1MiB, so every test of this cache had to build and redact a megabyte of realistic secret-bearing content** — and redaction is precisely the expensive thing. Measured locally under `-race`, those 17 tests cost **4m57s on their own**. CI's slower runners pushed the package past 600s.

Worth being precise about blame: **roughly half that cost predates this PR.** The #2002 tests were already ~150s under `-race`; mine doubled it and tipped it over. So main was slow here and I made it fail.

## The fix

The threshold is now a `var` so a test helper lowers it to 8KiB and restores it. That's honest rather than a dodge — the threshold is a production tuning constant; what these tests actually exercise is the splice logic. The one test that *does* care about the gate keeps its own small-vs-large sizes.

One gap that fix opened, so I closed it: with every test overriding the value, nothing would notice if the shipped default changed. There's now a test pinning it at 1MiB.

**Checkpoint package under `-race`: timed out at 10m → 20.7s.** Since the redaction tests were essentially the package's whole cost, this leaves it faster than main rather than merely recovered. Full `./cmd/entire/cli/...` under `-race` is clean, `lint` 0 issues, `test:ci` green.

Monitoring CI and I'll report when it lands.

Status:    open

Severity:  medium

Location: cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/redact_cache.go:239

Missing validation before dereferencing `entry.RedactedBlob`. When `entry.RedactedFile` is empty, the code assumes `entry.RedactedBlob` is non-empty and calls `plumbing.NewHash(entry.RedactedBlob)` without checking. The `load()` validation at lines 119-125 permits an entry where both are empty to pass (it only rejects when both are empty), but an entry with `RedactedFile=""` could have `RedactedBlob=""`. Add `if entry.RedactedBlob == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("entry has no blob reference") }` before calling `readBlobBytes`, or restructure `readPrefix` to validate the field it will use.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG'
fix(redact): validate the prefix field readPrefix is about to use

Trail finding on #2107 (medium). The reported dereference is not reachable:
load() rejects a record with neither RedactedFile nor RedactedBlob set, and
reusePrefix -- readPrefix's only caller -- returns early on a nil load. So an
entry reaching the blob branch always has a blob.

Adopting the fix anyway, because the reviewer is pointing at real fragility even
though the bug is not there. The guarantee lived 80 lines from the code relying
on it, and plumbing.NewHash("") does not fail loudly: it yields the zero hash and
surfaces as a puzzling missing-object error rather than a bad cache entry. Each
branch now checks its own field, and a test covers the shape by hand-writing an
entry storePrefix cannot express, confirming it degrades to a full redaction
rather than failing the checkpoint.

All 11 checks now pass. The remaining red was the Entire gate, which had picked up a real finding.

## The timeout fix worked

`test` and `test-core` are green. Checkpoint package under `-race`: **timed out at 10m → 22s.**

## The trail finding: not a bug, fixed anyway

`redact_cache.go:239`, Medium, 0.85 confidence — claimed a missing check before `plumbing.NewHash(entry.RedactedBlob)`.

**Its stated reachability is wrong.** The finding says `load()` "permits an entry where both are empty" and then that "an entry with `RedactedFile=""` could have `RedactedBlob=""`" — but `load()` rejects exactly that case, and `reusePrefix` (the only caller) returns early on a nil load. So an entry reaching the blob branch always has a blob.

I took the fix regardless, because the reviewer is pointing at real fragility even though the bug isn't there: the guarantee lived 80 lines from the code depending on it, and `plumbing.NewHash("")` doesn't fail loudly — it yields the zero hash and surfaces as a puzzling missing-object error rather than a bad cache entry. Each branch now validates its own field, with a test that hand-writes the shape `storePrefix` can't express and confirms it degrades to a full redaction rather than failing the checkpoint. Cheaper than arguing, and the code is genuinely better.

## One thing worth flagging about the toolchain

`mise run fmt` silently rewrote my `fmt.Errorf("…")` to `errors.New("…")` **without adding the import**, so the tree stopped compiling after a formatting pass. Lint reported `0 issues` on that broken tree — `go vet` was what caught it. That's a live trap: the project docs say to treat `fmt && lint` as one verification sequence, but neither step notices this. I only caught it because I run the race suite after linting.

`lint` 0 issues, `test:ci` green, 56+4 canary. `Entire Gates` should clear on the next run now the finding is addressed — it still needs your approval either way.
